title: The black box as a control for payoff-based learning in economic games

source.title: The black box as a control for payoff-based learning in economic games
source.authors: Maxwell N. Burton-Chellew; Stuart A. West

studies.title: Black boxes with hidden human groupmates (previously published data)
studies.description: Data from Burton-Chellew & West (2021): three short black boxes in which the hidden groupmates were other participants. Reanalysed here as the comparison group.

studies.title: Black boxes with hidden computerized groupmates (new experiment)
studies.description: New experiment, February 2020, CESS Oxford: five treatments (three short, two long) with computerized groupmates.

studies.title: Comparison of learning with hidden humans versus hidden computers
studies.description: Analysis scope comparing inputs and beliefs between the human-groupmate data and the computerized-groupmate data.

evidence.quote: Here we test a solution to this problem, in a range of public goods games, by making participants interact, unknowingly, with simulated players (‘computerized black box’). We find no significant differences in rates of learning between the original and the computerized black box.

The black box method was developed as an ‘asocial control’ to measure the potential role of payoff-based learning in social dilemmas [1]. Players must decide how many virtual coins they want to input into a virtual black box that will provide uncertain returns.
By ‘black boxing’ the game’s social aspects and payoffs, the method creates a population of self-interested but ignorant or confused individuals that must learn the games payoffs.
However, in reality, the experiment actually involved groups of real participants playing a typical public goods game, with all the usual payoffs and social connections, just unknowingly.

However, one potential critique of the black box is that because participants are interacting, albeit it unknowingly, the learning of one participant changes the learning environment for other participants.

Our solution is to make individuals still interact with a black box, but to change the set-up so that individuals are grouped not with each other, but with computerized players (computerized black box) (Figure 1).

They had one ‘easy’ learning condition with a small group size and low MPCR (N = 3 and MPCR = 0.4) and two ‘difficult’ learning conditions with either a large MPCR (N=3 and MPCR = 0.8) or large group size (N = 12 and MPCR = 0.4) [29]. However, instead of connecting human participants together, as done by Burton-Chellew & West, 2021[29], we use computerized groupmates (programmed to play randomly from a uniform distribution).
If behaviour with computerized black boxes qualitatively replicates behaviour with human black boxes, then the computerized black box method can be used to test hypotheses

Nevertheless, it may be that individuals just need more time to learn in these challenging conditions and will eventually learn to not contribute. To test this, we repeated the black boxes with the difficult learning conditions, but under two conditions, a short game and a long game (16 versus 40 rounds).

In all cases we measured learning in two ways; (1) how quickly incentivized contributions converged towards the Nash equilibrium of 0 contributions, and (2) by asking participants at the end of the experiment to report their belief about what was the best number to contribute (“input”) into the black box (this was unincentivized).
We analyzed previously published data from Burton-Chellew & West, 2021 [29] and compared these data with those from a new experiment with computerized black boxes.
The new experiment was conducted in February 2020 using 222 participants across 14 sessions over 3 days at the Centre for Experimental Social Sciences, Oxford (CESS).
CESS recruited the participants from their entire database with the sole restriction that they could not have participated in the prior study of Burton-Chellew & West, 2021 [29].

MNBC conducted the experiment proper in a laboratory with 25 computer stations. For each session we made 25 spaces available, and attendance varied from 7 to 25. The experiment was coded and conducted in z-TREE and participants were recruited using the ORSEE software [45, 46].

The total sample was 222 participants. Their age ranged from 18 to 81 years old. The mean ± SD was 31.8 years ±15.9 (N=192, this does not include seven participants that declined to answer nor all 23 participants from the first session). According to the self-reported genders, we had 139 females, 81 males, 1 other and 1 declined to answer.

Our design replicated the three ‘short’ treatments from Burton-Chellew, 2021 which varied both the group size (N) and the return from contributing (Marginal Per Capita Return, MPCR). We also added two ‘long’ treatments, played for 40 instead of 16 rounds. However instead of connecting real individuals with each other, we connected each participant with N-1 computerized virtual players that simulated random decisions drawn from a uniform decision. This way the payoff was entirely consistent with a public goods game, but players had no knowledge of the game and there were no ethical concerns of possible deception or lack of informed consent.

evidence.quote: Participants either played all three short treatments or one long treatment. When playing all three short treatments we counterbalanced the order across sessions (although not perfectly as the six permutations required a multiple of six sessions and we had eight). However here we only analyze the ‘naïve’ data from participants playing their first game.

The five treatments and naïve sample sizes were: Black box with N = 3 and MPCR = 0.4 first = 46 (over three sessions, 23, 11, 12); Black box with N = 3 and MPCR = 0.8 first = 44 (over three sessions, 22, 12, 10); Black box with N = 12 and MPCR = 0.4 first = 40 (over two sessions, 18 and 22); Black box with N = 3 and MPCR = 0.8 long version = 46 (over three sessions, 22, 7, 17); Black box with N = 12 and MPCR = 0.4 long version = 46 (over three sessions, 25, 9, 12)

The exchange rate was 0.65 pence to 1 virtual coin, except in the first session where it was 0.75. The total endowment was 960 coins (£6.24) in the short treatment sessions and 800 coins (£5.20) in the long treatments. Payments were rounded up to the nearest 10 pence. Earnings ranged from £8.20 to £16.90 (mean = £12.38), to which a £5 show up fee was added.

After each black box we asked participants two questions: (1) “Do you think there was a best number to put in this black box? Please enter 1 for 'Yes' and 0 for 'No'.”; and then (2) “If yes, what do you think was the best number (0-20)? If no, then please enter 99.”

Then after the experiment, we asked the participants to complete a brief survey on their self-reported gender, age, and personality traits, before asking them, “In a few words, please tell us what, if anything, you think the experiment was about?”.
All tests are two-tailed and we conducted all analyses in RStudio [47].

By testing behaviour in three different black boxes that varied in either group size (N = 3 or 12) or the marginal per capita return from contributing (MPCR = 0.4 or 0.8), they showed that a large group size and/or a high MPCR reduces the correlation between personal contributions and personal payoffs,

Welcome to the experiment!
A copy of these instructions is also available on-screen.
We are going to give you some virtual coins. Each 'coin' is worth real money.

You are going to make a decision regarding the investment of these 'coins'.
This decision may increase or decrease the number of coins you have.
The more coins you have at the end of the experiment, the more money you will
receive at the end.

At the end of the experiment the total amount of 'coins' you have earned will be
converted to pennies at the following rate: 100 coins = 65 pennies, or = £0.65.

In total, you will be given 960 coins £6.24 with which to make decisions and your
final total, which may be more or less than 960 coins, will depend on these
decisions.

The Decision
You will face the same decision many times. Each time we will give you 20
virtual 'coins'. Then you must decide on how many of your 20 coins to input into
a virtual 'black box'.

This 'black box' performs a mathematical function that converts the number of
'coins' inputted into a number of 'coins' to be outputted.

The mathematical function contains two components, one constant,
deterministic, component which acts upon your input, and one 'chance'
component.

You will play with this 'black box' for many rounds (more on this later), and the
mathematical function will not change, but the chance component means that if
you put the same amount of coins into the 'black box' over successive rounds,
you will not necessarily get the same output each time.

The number outputted may be more or less than you put in, but it will never be
a negative number, so the lowest outcome possible is to get 0 (zero) back.

If you chose to input 0 (zero) coins, you may still get some back from the black
box.

All coins not inputted into the black box will be automatically 'banked' into your
private account.
All coins outputted from the black box will also be 'banked' and go into your
private account.

evidence.quote: A copy of the instructions for the sessions with three short black boxes. For the long games the details were changed accordingly.
Table 1: Contributions over time. Analysis of how contributions (“inputs”) change during the game for each black box depending on if groupmates were humans or computers.
Table 2: Final contributions. Comparison of mean final round contributions (“inputs”) of virtual coins into the black box (0-20 coins). Comparisons made with Wilcoxon rank-sum test.
Table 3: Beliefs about the best number. The mean ±SE value participants stated as the best number to input at the end of the game.
Table 4. The effect of game length. Analysis of how inputs change during the game for each black box depending on game length (16 or 40 rounds).

Specifically, the game round x groupmates interaction was non-significant in all three black boxes (Generalized linear mixed models controlling for autocorrelation among groups/individuals: when N = 3 & MPCR = 0.4, Z = 0.2, P = 0.821; when N = 3 & MPCR = 0.8, Z=-1.2, P = 0.222; and when N = 12 & MPCR = 0.4, Z = -0.3, P = 0.760).

Specifically, when learning was easy (N = 3 & MPCR = 0.4), mean ±SE final round inputs (0-20 virtual coins) were 3.0 ±0.57 coins with humans and 4.7 ±0.90 coins with computers (Wilcoxon rank-sum test: W = 537, P = 0.797).

When learning was difficult, mean final round inputs were typically around 50% (10 virtual coins) with both humans and computerized groupmates (N = 3 & MPCR = 0.8, with humans = 10.1 ±0.91 coins, with computers = 9.4 ±1.12 coins, W = 573.5, P = 0.563; N = 12 & MPCR = 0.4, with humans = 10.3 ±0.89 coins, with computers = 9.7 ±1.12 coins, W = 128, P = 0.806).

Specifically, the mean ±SE stated beliefs (0-20 coins), for when N = 3 & MPCR = 0.4, were 1.5 ±0.79 coins with humans and 3.0 ±0.80 coins with computers (Wilcoxon rank-sum test, W = 348, P = 0.072); for when N = 3 & MPCR = 0.8, were 8.8 ±1.32 coins with humans and 8.9 ±1.59 coins with computers (W = 469.5, P = 0.888) and for when N = 12 & MPCR = 0.4, were 9.8 ±1.38 coins with humans and 8.0 ±1.37 coins with computers (W = 387, P = 0.349).
Overall, we found no significant differences between either inputs or beliefs depending on if individuals were grouped with humans or computers.

Overall, the estimated rate of decline was significantly negative in both black boxes (Table 4, generalized linear mixed model controlling for individual: when N = 3 & MPCR = 0.8, Z = -2.8, P = 0.005; when N = 12 & MPCR = 0.4, Z = -3.3, P < 0.001, depending on black box).

significantly different between the short and long games, suggesting that the rate of learning is relatively constant within these time frames despite being undetectable in the short games (Table 4, round x game length interaction: N = 3 & MPCR = 0.8, Z = 1.0, P = 0.308; N = 12 & MPCR = 0.4, Z = 0.5, P = 0.643).

Specifically, for the black box where N = 3 and MPCR = 0.8, mean ±SE final inputs were 9.4 ±1.12 coins in the short game and 6.2 ±0.97 coins in the long game (Wilcoxon rank-sum test, W = 1,287.5, P = 0.025).
and MPCR = 0.4, final inputs were 9.7 ±1.12 coins in the short game and 5.4 ±0.98 coins in the long game (W = 1,238.5, P = 0.006).

Specifically, the mean ±SE stated beliefs (0-20 coins), for when N = 3 & MPCR = 0.8, were 8.9 ±1.59 coins in the short game and 3.5 ±1.10 coins in the long game (Wilcoxon rank-sum test, W = 410.5, P = 0.010); for when N = 12 & MPCR = 0.4, were 8.0 ±1.37 coins in the short game and 4.0 ±0.93 coins in the long game (W = 496.5, P = 0.016).
Our results show clear evidence that participants are capable of payoff-based learning in public-goods games (Figures 2 & 4).
Another possible problem is that individuals unknowingly affect the payoffs of other participants, which may raise ethical concerns for some reviewers.
*An error prevented data collection from some participants in the first 7 sessions with human groupmates.

nodes.title: Overview

fields.label: Method type
fields.value: Laboratory economic-game experiments (repeated public-goods games presented as a 'black box'), plus reanalysis of previously published data

fields.label: Summary
fields.value: The paper tests whether replacing the hidden human groupmates of the original black box with computerized groupmates that play randomly changes how participants learn, and whether longer games reveal learning in difficult black boxes.

nodes.title: Payoff-based learning and the black box control

fields.label: Question
fields.value: Does the computerized black box (individuals grouped with computerized players) produce the same payoff-based learning as the original black box with hidden human groupmates?

fields.label: Gap
fields.value: In the original black box, participants unknowingly affect each other, so the learning of one participant changes the learning environment for others.

fields.label: Theory
fields.value: Repeated-game behaviour can be confounded by individuals responding to their payoffs and learning how to play; an asocial control separates payoff-based learning from social responses.

nodes.title: Black box payoff rule (structure from the paper's description)

fields.label: Output of the black box

value.output: MPCR × sum of the N inputs (own plus N−1 groupmates)

fields.derivation: Output = MPCR x sum of the N inputs (own plus N-1 groupmates) and income = 20 - own input + output. The paper says the payoff was entirely consistent with a public goods game with N-1 uniform random players, with MPCR the marginal per capita return; the output is therefore the MPCR share of the group's total input.

material.what: Black box output rule and groupmate draws
material.basis: The paper states the payoff was entirely consistent with a public goods game with N-1 uniform random computerized players and the MPCR of each treatment.

nodes.title: Procedure of the computerized black box experiment

fields.label: Task
fields.value: Each round the participant receives 20 coins and decides how many to input into a black box; the black box outputs coins, which are banked with the coins not input. 16 rounds (short) or 40 rounds (long), the same black box throughout.

fields.label: What the participant sees
fields.value: Instructions (also available on-screen), their own input and the black box output each round. Groupmates and the game's public-goods structure are hidden.

fields.label: Computerized groupmates' decisions
fields.value: Each of the N-1 computerized players draws its input at random from a uniform distribution each round; the range is taken as the integers 0-20 (the participants' own input range).
fields.derivation: Paper: 'simulated random decisions drawn from a uniform decision'; the 0-20 integer range is the participants' own input range, which the paper does not restate for the computers.

fields.label: Feedback
fields.value: After each round the participant receives the black box output ('You receive your output', banked).

fields.label: Belief questions
fields.value: After the last round of each black box, two unincentivized questions about the best number to input.

nodes.title: Findings

fields.label: Answer
fields.value: The authors report no differences in final inputs or beliefs between hidden human and computer groupmates, and no round-by-groupmate interactions. Table1 nevertheless reports a groupmate main effect for N=3,MPCR=.8 (p=.030), so the broad narrative null is not a claim that every model term is nonsignificant. Longer games yield lower final inputs and beliefs in difficult conditions, consistent with payoff-based learning.
